newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia targets Mostar mafia after attacks on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Croatia targets Mostar mafia after attacks on NATO.

text.p: Croatia has cracked down on Mostar's feared Croat warlords after Western warnings that attacks on NATO troops in the south Bosnian town threatened its wider interests, analysts said on Thursday.
Croatian police arrested the leader of Mostar's paramilitary mafia, Mladen Naletilic, alias Tuta, near Split on Monday, Croatian media said.
In a coordinated action against organised crime, Bosnian Croat police arrested five Croat men and issued warrants for another three on Wednesday.
Naletilic, a paramilitary commander during Bosnia's 1992-95 war, was arrested hours after Western diplomats met Croatian government officials.
The diplomats expressed their "strong concern" over the attacks on NATO-led peacekeeping troops in Mostar last week, when armoured vehicles were targeted twice with anti-tank missiles.
No one was hurt in the incidents, which both happened in the Croat sector of the city.
"Zagreb obviously recognises the dangers involved in attacking NATO troops," a diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.

"The Herzegovina mafia were doomed when they attacked NATO troops in Mostar, directly threatening long-term strategic interests of Croatia: entering the Partnership for Peace and eventually NATO," Croatian analyst Davor Gjenero said.

Naletilic and other paramilitaries are said to have made fortunes from racketeering, including evictions of Moslems, while exerting great influence over local politics and law enforcement, such as it was.
The arrests were seen as a major policy turnabout for the nationalist government of President Franjo Tudjman, the ultimate patron of the Bosnian Croats.
Croatian authorities have in the past appeared to tolerate, if not protect, the rogue elements in western Herzegovina who opposed normalising relations with Bosnian Moslems.

"Obviously, Croatian authorities have run out of patience with these people. It was visible for some time that they were trying to distance themselves from the Herzegovina hardliners," another Western diplomat said.

The United States ambassador to Croatia, Peter Galbraith, welcomed the move. "The arrest of mafia figures is clearly a positive signal and we hope that it will have a calming effect on the tensions in Mostar," he told Reuters.

Tensions in the divided southern town, contested by Moslems and Croats during their 1993-94 war, rose this month when Croat police fired on a group of Moslem civilians who wanted to visit a graveyard in the Croat part of town.
One Moslem civilian was killed and around 20 wounded.
An International Police Task Force (IPTF) report named a number of Croat policemen involved in the shooting, demanding that they be dismissed and prosecuted by February 26.
But the IPTF spokesman in Sarajevo, Alex Ivanko, said on Thursday that "as of now, we cannot confirm any dismissals or arrests of people that have been named in the IPTF report".
He said the arrests of paramilitary criminals and the IPTF report were two separate issues.
"The fact that the (Croat) authorities are cracking down on organised crime, if this is a crackdown, is extremely welcome and was long overdue," Ivanko said.

Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic, alias Stela, who was said by Croatian media to be on the run, were named last summer by international mediators in Mostar as the main obstacles to the peace process in southern Bosnia.

The move to tame Herzegovina hardliners will inevitably reflect on the position of their powerful main backer in Zagreb -- Croatian Defence Minister Gojko Susak, a native of the Herzegovina region, Croatian analysts said.
"Susak has let himself be seen in Naletilic's company at soccer games and similar occasions, and the fact that the latter was put away can only mean that Susak's position has weakened," Gjenero said.
